papers.title: Deprivation of dietary fiber promotes low-grade neuroinflammation and anxiety-like behavior in mice
papers.abstract: Background: Intestinal health is an important determinant of brain function in that an array of gut perturbants, especially those targeting microbiota, influence behavior. Fermentable dietary fiber nourishes gut microbiota and, consequently, promotes gut health. We hypothesized that depriving mice of fermentable dietary fiber would impact their brain and behavior. Methods: Male C57BL/6J mice were fed standard grain-based chow (GBC), a compositionally defined diet (CDD) which mimics macronutrient content of GBC but lacks fermentable fiber, or CDD supplemented with the fermentable fiber inulin (CDD+INU). Mice were subjected to behavioral testing 6-8 weeks later followed by analysis of the gut brain axis. Results: Relative to GBC-fed mice, CDD-fed mice exhibited low-grade gut inflammation and a reduction in open-field center exploration, signaling heightened anxiety-like behavior. CDD+INU fully reversed these abnormalities arguing they were a consequence of fiber deprivation. Analysis of the gut microbiome and serum metabolome showed that CDD+INU increased oxidative phosphorylation and immune suppressive metabolites. Flow cytometric and transcriptomic analyses of the brain revealed an array of pro-inflammatory alterations in myeloid cells, CD4+ T-cells, microglia and astrocytes in mice fed CDD but not CDD+INU. Most notably, microglia and astrocytes from mice fed CDD, but not CDD+INU, displayed reduced mitochondrial respiration and greater glycolytic activity. CDD, but not CDD+INU consumption also reduced the abundance of oligodendrocytes and neurons, and increased hippocampal pro-inflammatory gene expression. Conclusions: Deprivation of fermentable fiber results in coordinated changes in brain immune composition and glial metabolic state that is associated with increased anxiety-like behavior.

papers.title: Confidence: Its Measurement, Relation to Behavior, and Neural Representation
papers.abstract: Confidence (certainty/uncertainty about one's own decision) has attracted considerable attention in psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. Yet its relation to behavior remains unclear: Some treat confidence as a cause of behavior whereas others view it as a state controlled by environmental variables. The unobservable nature of confidence makes its measurement validation and analyses difficult. To tackle these issues, we developed a novel procedure combining a decision-making task, risk choices, and a post-task open-ended questionnaire. Point-gain/loss amounts for correct/incorrect decisions varied depending on choices between high-risk/high-return and low-risk/low-return. In the questionnaire, 90% of 16 participants reported feelings interpretable as certainty/uncertainty when making those risk choices despite no instruction about confidence, whereas 8% did so when the choices led to identical outcomes/returns. This suggests confidence is a state controlled by environmental contingencies rather than a cause of behavior. We also decoded changes in the state from electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging.

papers.title: Increased Cognitive Load Expands, Stabilizes, and Aligns Visual Representation Across the Human Brain
papers.abstract: Cognitive load refers to the mental effort required to perform a task. While previous research has extensively examined its detrimental effects on neural and behavioral performance, much less is known about how the brain actively adapts to heightened demands. Across two fMRI experiments involving visual n-back tasks, we identified several fundamental properties of this adaptive process. First, higher load enhanced and expanded visual representations beyond localized visual regions, leading to widespread visual coding. At the global scale, heightened load promoted cross-regional coordination by increasing representational alignment and strengthening information encoded in interregional functional connectivity patterns. Beyond facilitating stronger visual representation, increased load also reduced neural pattern variability, which led to more stable information coding. Finally, load was encoded independently of other task-relevant information as a separate brain state, supporting its overarching role in guiding visual processing. Together, these findings revealed that the brain adapts to heightened cognitive demands by globally reorganizing neural processing to support flexible cognition.

papers.title: Compositional computations in the primate frontal cortex
papers.abstract: A hallmark of intelligence is the ability to apply familiar operations to new inputs without relearning. How neural circuits carry a learned computation into states never visited during training remains unclear. Here we combined neural recordings, circuit modeling and human experiments to investigate compositional generalization. Monkeys learned to combine a start location with a displacement specified by the direction and duration of an optic-flow stimulus, then encountered novel combinations of these familiar inputs. Frontal population activity separated the computation into spatial and temporal components: start location and flow direction established the neural state, from which activity evolved along shared timing dynamics. Novel combinations elicited accurate responses when trajectories maintained this organization, whereas departures predicted systematic behavioral biases. Circuit models revealed a three-way alignment problem: input representations, recurrent dynamics and readout operations must jointly implement the required computation. Mismatches produced systematic biases that increased with distance from trained conditions. Humans exhibited similar biases when familiar sensory cues and spatial transformations were linked through an unfamiliar mapping. Together, these findings show how the coordination of reusable neural resources supports new computations, and how its disruption produces predictable failures of generalization.

papers.title: No Evidence of an Effect of a Single Mirror Visual Feedback Session on Subsequent Motor Imagery
papers.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) and mirror therapy, based on mirror visual feedback (MVF), are recommended as adjuncts to conventional therapies for upper limb rehabilitation after stroke. Both approaches activate sensorimotor cortical networks despite the absence of overt movement, and their concurrent application has been associated with enhanced neural activation. The present study investigated whether a single session of MVF modulates subsequent kinesthetic Motor Imagery (kMI)-related neural activity. EEG data from 38 healthy participants (MVF: n = 18; sham: n = 20) were analyzed in a mixed pre-post design. Participants performed kMI before and after either an MVF or sham intervention. Analyses focused on mu-band (8-12 Hz) event-related desynchronization (ERD) and its hemispheric lateralization. Although kMI reliably elicited stronger contralateral than ipsilateral mu ERD, MVF did not significantly affect subsequent kMI-related mu ERD or its hemispheric lateralization. These findings suggest that previously reported facilitatory effects of MVF on MI may be more closely related to concurrent application than to immediate aftereffects, while potential effects of repeated MVF exposure on subsequent MI remain to be investigated. These findings provide a foundation for future studies investigating how MVF and MI can be combined to optimize upper-limb stroke rehabilitation.

papers.title: Generalizable sex differences in functional brain organization follow the cortical hierarchy in youth
papers.abstract: It remains unknown if sex differences in human functional connectivity follow a generalizable overarching principle. Here, we tested whether sex differences in functional connectivity during childhood and adolescence are organized along the sensorimotor-association (S-A) axis, a cortical hierarchy spanning unimodal sensorimotor to transmodal association cortex. We analyzed four large-scale, independent datasets of youth ages 5-23 years (total N = 3,355). Across datasets, males showed greater connectivity between functional networks, whereas females showed greater connectivity within networks, most prominently within the default mode network. More broadly, the sensorimotor and association ends of the S-A axis were more segregated in females and more integrated in males. This difference extended to macroscale cortical organization: the cortical hierarchy was expanded in females relative to males along the principal gradient of functional connectivity. Together, these findings identify the S-A axis as a generalizable organizing principle of sex differences in functional brain organization during youth.

papers.title: Real-time detection of N2 and N3 sleep from scalp and intracranial EEG
papers.abstract: Sleep rhythms such as slow oscillations and spindles arise predominantly during N2 and N3 sleep (N2+N3). Closed-loop stimulation targeting these rhythms is a promising strategy to enhance memory. Such stimulation requires online sleep stage classification. Conventional staging labels completed 30-s epochs using past and future data and cannot support online staging. We developed a causal tracker that, every 2 s, estimates the current stage from the preceding 10 s of scalp or intracranial EEG. We also evaluated a simulated rule that permits stimulation after three consecutive estimates indicating N2+N3 sleep. In six adults with drug-resistant epilepsy with simultaneous scalp EEG and stereo-EEG, real-time N2+N3 discrimination remained close to offline scoring of the same recordings (scalp AUC 0.953 versus 0.958). Thalamic channels alone reached AUC 0.934 and exceeded mesial temporal channels in every patient, and scalp plus thalamus performed best (0.967). The scalp tracker, retrained in 28 healthy adults, reached 0.976. When patients transitioned into N2+N3 sleep with stimulation initially disabled, the rule permitted stimulation within 5 min in 63-73% of transitions, with a median delay of 42-64 s among those detected. After leaving N2+N3, stimulation was disabled after a median of 19-22 s. The rule also switched on incorrectly 1.4-1.8 times per hour outside N2+N3 and remained active during 28-31% of REM in patients, compared with 2% in healthy adults. These findings show that both scalp and thalamic EEG can support real-time N2+N3 detection and inform when stimulation is permitted. Translationally, implanted thalamic leads, increasingly used for neuromodulation in epilepsy, could support sleep-stage-dependent stimulation without scalp EEG, while scalp EEG might be used for noninvasive neuromodulation. Closed-loop systems should be evaluated not only by sleep-stage classification accuracy but also by how reliably and promptly they enable and disable stimulation.

papers.title: Measuring neuronal input-output operations in vivo with random access projection microscopy
papers.abstract: Neurons transform thousands of synaptic inputs into spiking output, and understanding this transformation requires measuring many submicron synapses at millisecond timescales in vivo. Here we present SLAP2, a two-photon random access projection microscope with no per-target access time cost, yielding over 5-fold faster imaging than existing methods, and performant real-time hardware motion correction. Flexible scanning modes enable measurement of hundreds of synapses at ~200 Hz, >800 synapses volumetrically at 50-100 Hz, and compartment-resolved dendritic voltage at 2-10 kHz in behaving mice. Simultaneous dendritic glutamate and somatic calcium imaging in visual cortex pyramidal neurons revealed nonlinear input-output amplification of stimulus onset and preferred stimulus orientation responses. Amplified features are associated with spatially organized inputs and stronger trial-to-trial coupling between synaptic activity and somatic output. These measurements establish SLAP2 as a powerful tool for recording intricate patterns of subcellular fluorescence dynamics in behaving animals.

papers.title: Sex-dependent and region-specific morphological adaptations in astrocytes following early-life stress
papers.abstract: Astrocytes are structurally heterogeneous, with cell morphology providing a valuable readout of experi-ence-dependent plasticity. Despite this, single-cell reconstruction including complete cellular territories remains challenging to compare across brain regions and experimental groups. We used unilateral retro-orbital delivery of PHP.eB-GfaABC1D-eGFP as a practical method for sparse astrocyte labeling and ap-plied it to evaluate regional, sex, and early-life-stress comparisons in the mouse amygdala. Systemic vi-rus delivery to broadly target astrocytes across the brain produced eGFP-positive cells throughout cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and amygdala with spatially isolated cells suitable for intensity projection, three-dimensional surface reconstruction, filament tracing, and Sholl analysis. In naive females, we report relatively homogenous morphological features between lateral amygdala and basal amygdala. In naive males, basal amygdala astrocytes had greater volume and a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio, while surface area, soma diameter, territory, and arborization measures did not differ significantly. Interestingly, early-life stress produced sex-specific morphological responses in the basal amygdala. Females showed increased perimeter, area, and Feret diameter without significant changes in three-dimensional volume or resolved filament measures. Males instead showed reduced surface area and volume, with no significant changes in projected territorial dimensions, soma diameter or resolved filament measures. S100{beta}-positive cell density was unchanged in the displayed regional and stress comparisons. These findings es-tablish systemic sparse eGFP labeling as an efficient route to single-cell astrocyte morphometry and re-veal a sex-dependent and region-specific dissociation between territorial expansion and three-dimensional volumetric contraction after early-life stress.

papers.title: Broad Cognitive and Motivational Enhancement through M4-Selective Muscarinic Modulation
papers.abstract: The muscarinic M4 subtype of acetylcholine receptors is part of agonist compounds considered treatment options for Schizophrenia and Alzheimers disease, but how M4-subtype selective modulation affects cognition and motivation is largely unknown due to dose-limiting side effects, a scarcity of receptor-selective compounds, and missing multi-domain assessments of cognition. Here, we surmount these constraints by utilizing a M4-selective positive allosteric modulator (PAM) to assess in nonhuman primates a broad array of endpoints spanning motivational effort control and multiple executive function domains. We found broad dose-dependent performance improvements of set shifting indexing cognitive flexibility, visual search indexing selective attention, antisaccade performance indexing inhibitory control, visuospatial maze learning, and temporal order serial object learning, while working memory span was non-systematically modulated. In addition, the M4 PAM reduced effort avoidance in an effort-based choice task documenting a pro-motivational effect. Task-composite performance scores showed pro-cognitive effects across multiple doses and an effective dose range for individual subjects in the absence of adverse dose-limiting cholinergic side effects. Together, the broad pro-cognitive and pro-motivational multi-task profile of M4 PAM modulation suggests that the M4 receptor is a master regulator of executive cognitive functioning, possibly acting on domain-general neural processes across the prefrontal-striatal circuits.

papers.title: Network analysis of mouse brain proteomes resolves molecular and cellular endophenotypes of aging and Aβ pathology
papers.abstract: Aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology exert both shared and distinct effects on the brain, yet their relative contributions to molecular alterations remain poorly defined. Here we performed tandem mass tag proteomics across the lifespan in wild-type and 5xFAD mice and integrated these data with human brain proteomic networks to resolve aging- and amyloid-beta (A{beta}-associated molecular programs. We quantified 8,535 proteins and identified 51 co-expression modules representing neuronal, mitochondrial, glial, vascular and proteostatic pathways. Aging emerged as the predominant driver of proteomic remodeling, with widespread alterations in RNA metabolism, protein translation, and neuronal pathways occurring independently of A{beta} pathology. In contrast, A{beta} selectively modified a subset of age-dependent processes, including suppression of mitochondrial ATP biosynthetic machinery and amplification of astrocytic and microglial activation states. These key aging and disease-related molecular signatures were highly conserved in human AD brain proteomes. Together, our findings establish aging as the primary determinant of brain proteome organization while revealing specific mechanisms through which A{beta} pathology reshapes age-associated biological processes. Our results also highlight molecular mechanisms of human aging and AD pathology that can be modeled in mouse models.

papers.title: Developmental interactions between oscillatory and spontaneous neural activity support improvements in inhibitory control from adolescence into adulthood
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period of development marked by improvements in cognitive control driven by maturation of executive brain systems. Neural mechanisms supporting inhibitory control (the ability to suppress a prepotent response in favor of generating a goal-directed response) mature into adulthood in parallel with refinements in frequency-specific neural oscillations and broadband spontaneous activity, supporting more accurate and reliable performance on response inhibition tasks, such as the antisaccade oculomotor task. Prior work has established that the maturation of neural circuitry contributes to age-related decreases in spontaneous activity, supporting higher-fidelity transmission of task-relevant activity, such as frequency-specific neural oscillations, which are crucial for antisaccade performance. Using longitudinal electroencephalography (EEG) data from 146 participants (72 F, ages 10-34, 253 total sessions) collected while participants performed an antisaccade task, we sought to understand the interplay between frontal oscillatory and spontaneous activity during cognitive processing and how it supports developmental improvements in inhibitory control. We found that spontaneous activity decreased developmentally during the preparation of an inhibitory response, and that this was associated with reduced trial-to-trial variability in response latency, indicating that reductions in spontaneous activity may increase the reliability of inhibitory control processing. Furthermore, performance-related decreases in broadband spontaneous activity were associated with the suppression of preparatory high-beta oscillations in an age-dependent manner, such that this relationship became more pronounced through development. Together, these results illustrate how developmental enhancements in the coordination of frequency-specific oscillations and spontaneous activity during inhibitory response preparation support developmental improvements in inhibitory control, providing a potential mechanism through which inhibitory control becomes more accurate and reliable from adolescence into adulthood.

papers.title: Therapeutic Potential of Melatonin, Erythropoietin, and TRPV4 Antagonism in a Preclinical Model of Genetic Hydrocephalus
papers.abstract: Symptomatic hydrocephalus is a neuropathological disorder of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) homeostasis characterized by abnormal accumulation of CSF and progressive ventricular enlargement. Current treatment relies primarily on surgical CSF diversion, which is invasive and associated with substantial rates of treatment failure and surgical revisions. Congenital hydrocephalus can be caused by genetic pathologies; for example, a point mutation in the Meckel-Gruber type 3, Tmem67, gene produces a congenital hydrocephalus phenotype in rats, characterized by progressive ventriculomegaly. Here, we evaluated a combinatorial cocktail therapeutic strategy consisting of erythropoietin (EPO), melatonin (MLT), and the transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4) antagonist, RN1734 (RN), in the Tmem67-- rat model of congenital hydrocephalus. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrated marked progression of ventriculomegaly in untreated Tmem67-- rats between postnatal (P) 7 and P15. RN1734 and EPO+MLT+RN1734 (triple therapy) from P7-P14 prevented further ventricular expansion. Hydrocephalus is associated with structural disruption of the periventricular white matter (WM) and ependymal lining (EL), accompanied by regionally increased TLR4 and NLRP3-associated inflammatory signaling. EPO+MLT, RN1734, or triple therapy differentially attenuated these inflammatory responses. The triple combination reduced both TLR4 and NLRP3 protein abundance within the affected periventricular region and ameliorated the structural alterations. These findings support a combined therapeutic approach that addresses ventricular pathology, inflammation and periventricular structural consequences of congenital hydrocephalus.

papers.title: Human organoid screen links transient translational modulation to progenitor progression in corticogenesis
papers.abstract: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived models are increasingly used to recapitulate aspects of human corticogenesis, including the emergence of diverse cortical cell types and their progression through developmental states. These systems offer an opportunity to dissect the molecular mechanisms regulating transitions between cell states, but methods for perturbing them systematically at scale remain limited. Here, we developed a semi-automated culture and high-throughput arrayed screening platform for human cortical organoids. Using a library of 1,280 small molecules designed to systematically target major signaling and regulatory pathways, we screened for modulators of EOMES, which encodes for the transcription factor TBR2, and identified Emetine, an inhibitor of translation elongation, as the top hit. The effect of Emetine on cortical cell-state progression was reproduced across human pluripotent stem cell lines, non-human primate cortical organoids, and primary human cortical tissue but not broadly across translation inhibitors. Moreover, transient exposure resulted in a shift from dividing radial glia towards cortical glutamatergic neurons. Mechanistically, nascent-proteome profiling revealed an early and coordinated remodeling of newly translated proteins that preceded detectable transcriptional changes, placing translational regulation upstream of the ensuing cell-state transition. Together, these findings highlight a role for specific translational inhibitors in promoting cortical cell-state progression and establish a scalable platform for systematic perturbation and discovery in human neural organoids.

papers.title: Brief visual oddball events evoke CSF flow in the spinal canal
papers.abstract: The measurement of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow with fMRI, made possible by exploiting edge artifacts of spin saturation when the bottom acquisition slice lies in a CSF reservoir, allows researchers to investigate an aspect of brain health that has been increasingly linked to cognitive aging and neurodegenerative disease via its role in glymphatic clearance. The initial demonstration of this technique used the fourth ventricle, but recent reports show it can also be done when the bottom acquisition slice lies in the spinal canal in the foramen magnum. We present a method to automatically identify the spinal canal without manual tracing, and measure CSF flow with high confidence using multi-echo acquisition to separate out BOLD-like and non-BOLD-like signal components, along with physiological regression to improve signal to noise ratio. Using these methods we found that CSF flow correlated with decreases in BOLD activity in 70 adults aged 19-76. We further found that brief, infrequent salient stimuli (visual oddballs, requiring a button press) were capable of provoking measurable CSF flow.

papers.title: Tyrosine hydroxylase deletion in Ntsr1 neurons confers resistance to diet-induced weight gain: an energy-balance analysis
papers.abstract: High-fat diet (HFD) disrupts circadian feeding rhythms and promotes diet-induced obesity (DIO), but the neural mechanisms linking diet to energy balance remain unclear. Previously, we demonstrated that dopamine production in neurotensin receptor 1 (Ntsr1)-expressing neurons was required for HFD-induced daytime overfeeding and DIO. Here, we tested whether DIO resistance in Ntsr1Cre;Thflox conditional knockout (cKO) mice was explained by altered energy expenditure. We replicated resistance to HFD-induced weight gain and assessed food intake, indirect calorimetry, activity, body temperature, fecal energy, fecal nonesterified fatty acids, and the gut microbiome. Indirect calorimetry on standard chow diet (SCD) was confounded by reduced intake and body weight loss, whereas HFD-fed cKO mice consumed food readily and resisted weight gain. Unlike our previous study, daytime feeding was not suppressed; instead, cKO mice were slightly and variably hypophagic on HFD but not SCD. DIO resistance was not accompanied by increased energy expenditure, activity, or body temperature. Rather, cKO mice showed reduced energy expenditure and activity and lower body temperature on both diets. In the replication cohort, HFD fecal output was lower in cKO mice, whereas the independent bomb-calorimetry cohort showed no genotype difference in fecal mass; fecal energy density and nonesterified fatty acid concentration were unchanged. Preliminary analysis of the microbiome was consistent with an obesity-resistant gut profile. Together, these findings indicate that the feeding phenotype is diet- and experiment-dependent and that DIO resistance is not explained by increased energy expenditure, activity, thermogenesis, or detectable changes in fecal energy or fat content.

papers.title: Druggable CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory axis links Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome with MECP2-related disorders
papers.abstract: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) abundance. Too little causes Rett syndrome (RTT), too much causes MECP2 duplication syndrome (MDS), and in both, severity tracks with the amount of functional MeCP2. Even modest deviations are detrimental, yet how MeCP2 abundance is controlled remains poorly understood. Using genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens, we identified hundreds of proteins regulating MeCP2, revealing a casein kinase 2 alpha 1 (CSNK2A1)-driven regulatory axis stabilizing MeCP2. We show this axis is druggable and therapeutically relevant, using a novel CSNK2A1 inhibitor in human cells and targeting Csnk2a1 in an MDS mouse model. We further connect CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory disruption to Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), caused by mutations in CSNK2A1, finding ~50% less hippocampal MeCP2 in an OCNDS mouse model. Together, these data identify a druggable regulatory axis modulating MeCP2 and implicate MeCP2 dysregulation in the molecular pathogenesis of OCNDS and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders.

papers.title: Motivation-dependent communication between cortex and brainstem
papers.abstract: Neurons in the medullary brainstem exhibit movement-related patterns of activity, but the neuronal population codes that specify distinct actions, and the mechanisms by which cortex may shape these codes as a function of motivational state, remain unclear. To explore whether coupling between cortex and medulla depends upon motivational context, we trained mice to make both pre-reward "appetitive" licks that served to trigger water availability and rapidly attenuated with satiety, and "consummatory" licks, which occur post-reward release and more slowly attenuated with satiety. Simultaneous recordings from secondary motor cortex and motor medulla revealed that medullary activity was more time-locked than cortical activity to individual licks and exhibited a phase-based population code that encoded lick direction. Correlations between cortex and medulla were stronger during appetitive licks than during consummatory licks, with causal dependency established by optogenetic intervention and supported by multi-region recurrent network models. Population codes underlying behavior shared across the central nervous system, exemplified by cortico-medullary coupling, thus may depend upon the motivational context underlying action.

papers.title: Next generation Human Neocortical Neurosolver model with biophysically realistic somatic, dendritic and synaptic dynamics
papers.abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca2+) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate how the updated circuitry and new features in the HNN software can be used to disentangle somatic, synaptic, and dendritic contributions to human E-/MEG signatures. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. These enhancements allow extensive model validations based on in vitro and in vivo electrophysiology, voltage and Ca2+ imaging, and provide users with novel insights on the mechanisms underlying E-/MEG signals.

papers.title: Persistent hippocampal traces of lifelong spatial memory
papers.abstract: Memory presents a biological paradox: the brain changes continuously, yet a brief experience can influence behavior for a lifetime. How such memories are stored in brain circuits remains unclear. Here we show that two days in a binary-tree maze leave mice with spatial memories that survive repeated 90-day absences over as much as a year. Across return visits, mice explored the maze more efficiently than when naive and resumed direct runs to a reward location sooner, both by a factor of 3. Chronic calcium imaging of the same hippocampal CA1 neurons showed that although most neurons had changed their preferred locations, the population activity at a given maze location still resembled the pattern from 90 days earlier. Furthermore, even when a neuron's place fields changed location, they tended to remain at the same branching level of the binary tree, reflecting the local geometry of the maze. In return sessions where the neural tuning for branching level was preserved more accurately, the mouse explored the environment more efficiently. Population patterns were best preserved near the reward location, and more reliable neural activity there accompanied earlier direct runs to the reward. With repeated experience, spatial representations changed less, both within a visit and across the long absences. A brief experience thus left selective hippocampal traces that survived months of absence despite drift, grew more durable with each return, and were correlated with memory in navigation behavior.

papers.title: A biological light sheet links cellular voltage to mesoscopic brain dynamics
papers.abstract: Membrane voltage is the fundamental currency of neural computation, yet cellular-resolution voltage imaging of large neuronal populations in vivo remains limited by trade-offs among imaging speed, field of view, and optical sectioning. We overcome this challenge by encoding a biological light sheet in the brain: Selective Plane Expression (SPress) restricts fluorescent indicator expression to a user-defined, 20-m-thick plane, suppressing background at its source. Following one-time two-photon photoactivation, SPress enables standard widefield microscopes to capture high-contrast kilohertz voltage dynamics from hundreds of densely labeled neurons across millimeter-scale cortical sheets and columns in vivo. These recordings reveal mesoscopic subthreshold waves that flexibly reorganize population-wide spike timing, together with cellularscale wavefront microstructure that preserves stereotyped local recruitment biases. By shifting optical sectioning from instrumentation to gene expression, SPress makes kilohertz cellular resolution voltage imaging accessible across mesoscopic scales.

papers.title: Curved geometry shapes the observability of hippocampal oscillations
papers.abstract: Curved neural architectures reshape the spatial distribution of field oscillations, complicating the identification of their underlying generators. To test these principles experimentally, here we resolve the paradoxical poor expression of theta oscillations in the hilus of the folded dentate gyrus (DG), a region that otherwise exhibits some of the largest FPs in the brain. Using laminar recordings across both hippocampi and computational modeling, we show that theta is locally masked by cancellation of phase-coherent contributions. Theta generators in CA1 and DG produce volume-conducted fields that, due to the curved geometry of the DG, exhibit opposite dipolar orientations in the hilus, leading to regional cancellation. In contrast, beta and gamma generators are only weakly coordinated across hippocampal regions and therefore remain prominently expressed despite the same geometry. These results demonstrate that theta amplitude, local observability, spatial segregation and apparent translocation emerge from the interplay between geometry and temporal coherence among distributed generators, with tissue geometry acting as a spatial filter for coherent activity.

papers.title: A Framework for SPICE MRSI Reconstruction Posterior Uncertainty Quantification
papers.abstract: Purpose: Low-rank reconstruction methods such as SPICE substantially improve Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopic Imaging (MRSI) reconstruction quality. However, SPICE does not provide an estimate of reconstruction uncertainty. A framework for posterior uncertainty estimation in SPICE reconstruction is proposed, hereafter referred to as the framework. Theory and Methods: A Laplace approximation is used to estimate the covariance of the reconstructed spatial coefficients. This covariance is propagated through the spectral basis and spectral fitting to obtain metabolite concentration uncertainty. Matrix-free Hessian--vector products and voxel-wise conjugate-gradient estimation are used to avoid explicit construction or inversion of the full Hessian, making the method tractable. Results: Validation using repeated in vivo 7 T MRSI acquisitions showed that the estimated posterior uncertainty exhibited spatial and spectral patterns similar to those of empirical repeated-scan uncertainty. Experiments further demonstrated how spatial regularization and k-space undersampling affect the estimated uncertainty. Conclusion: The framework provides a practical framework for uncertainty quantification when using SPICE reconstruction of MRSI. It could be adapted to other regularised low-rank reconstruction methods.

papers.title: Neonatal NMDA receptor blockade disrupts prefrontal cortical regulation of social affective behavior: implications for schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Developmental N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAr) hypofunction has been implicated in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia, including cognitive and emotional deficits. However, the neural circuit mechanisms linking developmental NMDAr hypofunction to social affective impairments remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated schizophrenia-related social affective dysfunction induced by neonatal exposure to the NMDAr antagonist MK-801 and examined the contribution of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a key hub for socio-cognitive function. Sprague-Dawley rat pups received subcutaneous injections of saline or MK-801 (MK-Low: 0.2 mg/kg; MK-High: 0.4 mg/kg) during the neonatal period. In adulthood, social affective behaviors were assessed using the Social Affective Preference (SAP) and Social Interaction (SI) tests. MK-801-treated rats, particularly the MK-High group, displayed impaired social affective responses, characterized by reduced preference for and investigation of distressed conspecifics. These impairments were ameliorated by chemogenetic inhibition of pyramidal cells in the mPFC, whereas activation of these neurons disrupted social affective behavior in naive rats. Histological analyses revealed reduced parvalbumin-positive interneuron (PVIN) density in the mPFC of MK-801-treated rats. Consistent with the involvement of PVIN dysfunction, selective activation of mPFC PVINs alleviated social affective deficits in MK-801-treated rats. These findings identify impaired PVIN-mediated inhibitory regulation within the mPFC as a circuit mechanism underlying social affective dysfunction following neonatal NMDAr blockade, providing insight into the pathophysiology of schizophrenia-related social impairments.

papers.title: Walking delays auditory processing in humans alongside a global shift in aperiodic neural activity
papers.abstract: Natural sensory processing unfolds during movement, yet human electrophysiology is usually measured under enforced stillness. Here, we used mobile EEG to test whether walking changes the timing of auditory processing. Thirty adults listened to lateralised pure tones while walking freely or standing. Walking led to a delay in auditory N1 latency (< 10 ms). Control analyses ruled out the possibility that the N1 delay was contaminated by foot strike related noise in EEG. Multivariate decoding further indicated a later emergence of sound location information during walking in the subset of participants with reliable decoding in both states. Walking also produced a scalp wide decrease in the aperiodic exponent of neural responses. A larger global exponent decrease was associated with a larger N1 delay across participants. Together, these findings show that natural walking reorganises the temporal dynamics of human auditory processing and link early sensory slowing to a global change in ongoing cortical state.

papers.title: Extended Pavlovian conditioned approach training and devaluation in Long-Evans rats using time-restricted feeding
papers.abstract: Pavlovian conditioned approach (PCA) is a useful tool in studying compulsive- and addictive-like behaviors. PCA pairs a cue with reward delivery and rats typically differentiate into three phenotypes (sign-trackers, goal-trackers, and intermediates) based on behavior during the reward-paired cue presentation. Sign-trackers, who preferentially interact with the cue, are more likely to engage in compulsive behaviors and have decreased behavioral flexibility compared to goal-trackers, who preferentially interact with the food cup. However, one limitation to PCA is the use of food deprivation conditions that maintain rats at 80-90% of ad libitum weight, likely increasing stress which may bias animals towards sign-tracking behavior. Furthermore, most behavioral analysis only examines lever pressing and food cup entry, overlooking other behaviors that may better define phenotypes. In the current study male and female Long-Evans rats underwent an extended PCA training paradigm followed by satiety-induced reward devaluation under time-restricted feeding (TRF) conditions. Under TRF, rats continued to gain weight across PCA training and maintained caloric intake relative to ad libitum intake. Expanding the scope of behavioral analysis increased the proportion of ST rats in both early and late PCA training. Rats also increased the time spent interacting with the food cup during the inter-trial interval across extended PCA training. All rats were sensitive to satiety-induced reward devaluation, regardless of sex or devaluation condition. This study helps establish a PCA method optimized for Long-Evans rats with relevance for identifying PCA phenotypes contribution to dysregulated behavior in the context of chronic stress and obesity.

papers.title: Towards an analytical framework for investigating the neurophysiological influence of social context in speech perception
papers.abstract: Social information plays an important role in everyday speech communication, yet existing neurophysiological approaches provide limited means of isolating its contribution during naturalistic speech perception. Here, we present an analytical framework that combines the large language model (LLM) Mistral-Instruct, fine-tuned on conversational language, and temporal response functions (TRFs) to investigate the influence of social context on word-level speech processing. The framework disentangles local context (LC) from speaker-specific social context (SC) when generating LLM-derived lexical expectation measures, enabling such predictions to be generated under either matching or mismatching speaker contexts for the same speech material. This provides a direct way of isolating the contribution of social information to lexical predictions. We first show that speaker-related social context carries information about speech register and conversational role beyond that available from previous local context alone by interrogating Mistral-Instruct. We then demonstrate that lexical expectations generated from socially congruent contexts produce small but reliable improvements in EEG prediction relative to expectations generated from incongruent social contexts. These effects were observed despite identical acoustic input and neural recordings, indicating that the influence of social context on lexical expectations explains dissociable variance in neural responses to speech. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept for using LLM-derived lexical expectations to isolate and measure the influence of social context on speech processing. More broadly, the proposed framework offers a flexible approach for generating and testing hypotheses about how different forms of contextual knowledge shape neural responses during naturalistic language comprehension.

papers.title: Cross-excitation in dorsal root ganglia redistributes coding capacity from stimulus intensity to stimulus location
papers.abstract: The phenomenon of cross-excitation between neurons of dorsal root ganglia (DRGs) of mammals is widely known, yet its exact mechanism remains underexplored. In this work, we analyze the phenomenon as part of the signal processing performed by the body's somatosensory system. We argue that, if the mechanism is indeed as prevalent as it is reported in experimental works, it should provide a significant computational advantage. Here, we created a model network in which sensory A-type neurons are interconnected only via a chemical agent and showed that such a connection, when fitted with parameters similar to those observed in experiments, improves the stimulus-localization properties of the ganglia at the expense of intensity-encoding accuracy. Although this exchange is near-neutral in raw bits, it becomes favorable once the logarithmic compression of intensity perception - the Weber--Fechner law - is taken into account, since the sacrificed intensity capacity is largely perceptually redundant. We therefore propose that cross-excitation is not an imperfection of somatic isolation but an effective, chemically mediated pre-processing stage that sharpens spatial localization.

papers.title: Reinforcement sculpts synaptic ensembles for operant dendritic control
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning requires the selective modification of synapses that contribute to outcome-relevant neural activity, yet the principles underlying these selective modifications remain unclear. Here we combined longitudinal two-photon imaging of identified dendritic spines with a closed-loop optical brain-machine interface (BMI), in which activity from selected apical dendrites of layer 5 motor-cortical neurons controlled an auditory cursor, with target acquisition triggering optogenetic reinforcement. Mice learned to reliably generate the specific dendritic activity that leads to reinforcement. Learning was accompanied by selective strengthening and weakening of individual spines on reinforced dendrites. At individual synapses, the direction of plasticity depended on both the timing of activity relative to reinforced dendritic events and the pre-existing temporal organization of that activity. Furthermore, plasticity was enriched in small task-relevant synaptic groups: spines in synergistic groups were preferentially strengthened, whereas those in antagonistic groups were preferentially weakened. These changes were accompanied by the emergence of increasingly reproducible, selectively recruited, and temporally focused synaptic ensembles, and the incorporation of newly formed spines into these ensembles. Finally, blocking striatal dopamine receptor signaling impaired BMI learning and cortical synaptic reorganization of target dendrites, demonstrating a role for striatal reinforcement in cortical plasticity. Together, these findings reveal how reinforcement of specific dendritic activity sculpts synaptic ensembles that support learned operant dendritic control.

papers.title: Circuit and cell-type mechanisms of the spectrolaminar motif of cortical oscillations
papers.abstract: Oscillations are a key feature of cortical activity, coordinating spike timing across areas, layers, and cell types. Recent work suggests these rhythms follow a stereotyped organization across cortical depth, the spectrolaminar (SL) motif, with higher-frequency gamma prominent in superficial layers and lower-frequency alpha/beta in deep layers, yet the mechanisms generating it remain poorly understood. Using a bio-realistic model of mouse primary visual cortex, we reproduced the SL motif and found it preserved across diverse visual stimuli. Systematic cell-type- and layer-resolved perturbations showed that the alpha/beta component was intrinsic to every layer, whereas the 50-80 Hz gamma component was predominantly generated within layer 4 (L4) and propagated network-wide through inter-laminar connections. Pvalb interneurons were the principal regulators of gamma, Sst cells shaped low-frequency power, and Vip cells controlled oscillation magnitude. The temporal properties of L4 Pvalb-to-excitatory synapses were especially influential in generating the SL motif. These models and simulation results thus offer a plausible description of circuit mechanisms underlying cortical oscillations and the SL motif and are publicly available to facilitate further studies.
